passages.title: About Craig
passages.text: Craig Thompson 20+ years’ experience in software development and management, from start-up to acquisition. I’m a hands-on, full-stack engineer across UI, back end, infrastructure and AI, with extensive engineering leadership experience. I led an engineering department to AI-first development, where most code is now generated by AI, then reviewed by AI and people. Problem solving is what I do best, whether the problem sits in the code, the platform or the team. I’ve led engineering teams for 12+ years, growing and developing teams of 10+ engineers, both in-house and outsourced. I’ve set strategy, supported the people and steered the platform with them, from monorepos and build engines to AWS, authentication and AI tooling. I’ve reported directly to CEO and CTO level, turning the roadmap and technical direction into plain-English board updates. I’ve been part of ISO 27001 and GDPR accreditation and the annual audits.

passages.title: ai.md: From AI-assisted to AI-first, in a year
passages.text: Over the past year I've led a radical change in how an engineering department works, from first introducing AI-assisted development to a point where the vast majority of code is generated by AI and reviewed by AI alongside human reviewers. It's checked against style and coding guidelines iterated on in the repo, so what's produced meets the team's standards rather than the model's defaults. We started with AI-assisted coding (GitHub Copilot and Amazon Q) for routine tasks, before moving to AI-first development. Most code is now written by AI and checked by both AI and people before it merges. Standards live in the repo, so the models and the team work to the same rules. Claude rates every pull request green, amber or red, so reviewers know where to look before they open a diff. Terraform plans get an AI summary as a GitHub check before anyone approves them. Chores like cost audits, dataset restores and stacked PRs are one command for any engineer or agent, through 20+ Claude Code skills. passages.title: monorepo.md: One codebase, kept modern without stopping delivery
passages.text: // monorepo & developer experience · 2019; today One codebase, kept modern without stopping delivery I’ve taken a platform spread across about 18 separate repositories and led merging them into one TypeScript monorepo with their history intact, along with the tooling around it: CI/CD, Docker and local dev. That one codebase is what makes the repo-wide migrations in refactor.md possible. 2019 · 18 repositories 12 services React app 3 Lambdas Terraform QA suite today · one monorepo 100+ packages today, including the shared React design system Every engineer works in one repo, with one toolchain and one way to build, test and deploy. Generated OpenAPI 3.1 docs for 12 services replaced a hand-maintained Postman collection.

passages.title: refactor.md: Keep the toolchain modern, one reviewed change at a time
passages.text: // refactors & tooling migrations Keep the toolchain modern, one reviewed change at a time Tooling ages fast. Rather than letting it drift, I’ve led a steady run of repo-wide migrations: linting, packages, bundling, types, runtime and the compiler itself. Each one was scripted with a codemod and landed as a single reviewed change, so there was never a long-lived branch or a half-migrated codebase. Repo-wide migrations I've led9,700+ files moved across them linting TSLint ESLint 455 files ci Semaphore self-hosted Buildkite CI as code packages yarn pnpm workspaces 619 files bundling Webpack Vite 3 front ends types type aliases interfaces 804-file codemod lint + format ESLint + Prettier oxlint + oxfmt 4,366 files runtime compiled JS TypeScript run natively by Node 3,502 files compiler TypeScript 5.8 TypeScript 7 ~10× faster typechecks e2e testing Cypress Playwright faster, more stable CI Upgrades land across the repo in one change, so the codebase doesn’t drift into “old” and “new”. Back-end services start straight from TypeScript source, with no build step in between. Faster tools where it counts: one quick linter and formatter, and typechecks around 10× faster on TypeScript 7.

passages.title: ci-cd.md: Build only what changed, ship every merge
passages.text: // ci/cd & release engineering · 2019; today Build only what changed, ship every merge I built a CI/CD platform from scratch and have kept evolving it as the team and codebase grew. Today it runs on self-hosted Buildkite defined in Terraform, driven by an in-house TypeScript build-and-deploy engine. It models the monorepo’s dependency graph, so each change builds and deploys only the packages it affects. Every merge to master, end to end merge to master package graph what's affected? build in parallel affected packages only lib service app Validate gate format lint types tests drift staging auto-deploy production live, no release train How it evolved: pipelines; a graph-aware release engine hosted pipelines Buildkite + build engine continuous deployment merge queue · staging one Validate gate Merged work reaches customers automatically. There has been no release train since 2022. A small fix rebuilds a handful of packages, not the whole platform. Every PR passes one required quality gate, and /deploy on a PR puts it into a test environment. Deploys wait for healthy tasks and detect rollbacks, so a bad release stops itself.

passages.title: aws.md: Nothing public but the CDN
passages.text: // aws architecture · 2021; 2026 Nothing public but the CDN I led the platform’s move from containers on EC2 hosts behind a public load balancer to Fargate tasks that talk over ECS Service Connect, with all customer traffic entering through CloudFront and WAF. Each step shipped without a big-bang cutover. before · ~2020 Internet Public load balancer · internet-facing ECS on EC2 hosts · hosts to patch Database via VPC peering Operator access: SSH bastion after · 2026 Internet CloudFront + WAF · the only public entry Internal load balancer · private Fargate · Service Connect · no hosts Database via PrivateLink Operator access: SSO + SSM, no SSH How it evolved: hosts to patch; no hosts at all ECS on EC2 hosts capacity autoscaling awsvpc networking Fargate rollout Fargate + Service Connect No servers to patch: every service runs on Fargate. The attack surface is one CDN. WAF moved to blocking only after a 14-day shadow run showed no legitimate traffic would be stopped. Each service receives only the events it handles, using subscription filters generated from its code at build time. Dev environments share one networking stack and one database cluster, so a new environment is cheap to stand up.

passages.title: security.md: Closing doors, not adding locks
passages.text: // security & privacy · 2021; 2026 Closing doors, not adding locks When a product handles confidential data, security and privacy are part of the product. We focused on removing whole classes of risk rather than layering controls on top. areabeforeafter server accessSSH & bastionsSSM Session Manager; port 22 closed everywhere admin accessIAM admin usersSSO only, via IAM Identity Center and Control Tower networksVPC peeringPrivateLink and VPC endpoints public surfaceinternet-facing load balancerOne CDN entry point, with WAF in block mode dev secretsplaintext.env filesInjected at runtime from a password manager dependenciesknown CVEs lingeringVulnerable packages swapped out; pentest findings fixed and tracked incidentsad hocBlameless post-mortems, with runbooks and tooling as the fix Far fewer standing keys and passwords for anyone to leak. No servers reachable from the internet except through the CDN. External penetration-test findings were fixed in code and tracked to closure.

passages.title: auth.md: Sign-in that enterprises trust and users don't notice
passages.text: // authentication & identity · 2024; 2026 Sign-in that enterprises trust and users don't notice I led the replacement of a legacy, multi-tenant sign-in system with a new auth framework, rolled out organisation by organisation behind a per-tenant switch. Before that, we hardened the old one: expiring tokens, central signing and key rotation. Every sign-in, end to end sign-in request from a tenant domain resolve organisation from the host name choose a method SAML SSO magic link password 2FA enforced per org rate-limit check per identity session + signed token EdDSA · published keys rate limiting by identity, not just IP Separate buckets per user, email, token and IP, per organisation, so one noisy office network can't lock out everyone behind it. zero-downtime key rotation Verifiers accept old and new keys during an overlap window, so signing keys rotate without logging anyone out. How it evolved: legacy service; enterprise-grade sign-in legacy auth service shared auth library expiring, rotated tokens new auth framework Enterprise customers sign in through their own identity provider and can require 2FA for everyone. Sign-in links in emails still work after Slack or Outlook previews them. Tokens expire and keys rotate on a schedule, with no forced logouts. Services can verify tokens themselves against published keys, ready for service-to-service auth.

passages.title: data.md: Making the flagship report fast at scale
passages.text: // data & performance · 2021; 2026 Making the flagship report fast at scale Reporting is often the first place a SaaS platform slows down: large aggregations sliced by many dimensions at once. I led the redesign of a core reporting data model and its queries on MongoDB, and we proved the new version matched the old one in production before switching over. before: work done at read time, on every request every response unwind all facets group everything confidentiality in the query after: work moved to write time, reads stay lean facets denormalised on write purpose-built collection high-cardinality-first index analytics-node read confidentiality in code, cacheable 10× higher complexity ceiling for core reports 1–3 s search stalls removed from people lists under load ~8,000 records no longer loaded to open one dashboard V1 ⇄ V2 diff mode proved parity in production How it evolved: read-time work; write-time design streamed bulk operations reporting rework purpose-built collection Atlas Search Large customers can slice results by far more demographics before hitting limits. Bulk operations on very large tenants stream records instead of loading them all into memory. Every environment, and every laptop, can restore a realistic “gold” dataset in one step.

passages.title: cost.md: Measure first, then cut

Each change landed with the numbers that justified it in the pull request. measure attribute change verify Documented monthly AWS savings≈ $1.3k / month from the first three alone Container Insights: enhanced; standard $620/mo Duplicate CloudTrail trails removed $450/mo BI network: 3 AZs and NATs; 1 $270/mo VPC flow logs off (per account) $250/mo Also cut, from measured utilisation Traced ~1.2 TB/day of CI NAT traffic; replaced managed NAT with endpoints, image caching and fck-nat Halved CPU and memory on services idling at 1–3% CPU Right-sized Redis after 15 months under 4% CPU Non-production environments scale down every night Spend tracks real usage, and every cut has the evidence behind it on record. passages.title: webmcp.md: A site AI agents can use, not just read

passages.title: FAQ: What roles are you open to?
passages.text: Hands-on technical leadership roles, such as Head of Engineering, where I stay close to the code and to AI-first delivery while setting direction for the team. I’m most at home in start-ups and scale-ups.

passages.title: FAQ: Remote, hybrid or office?
passages.text: Primarily remote. I’d consider hybrid for a North East–based company with genuinely flexible attendance, but not a fixed “X days a week” commitment.

passages.title: FAQ: Where are you based?
passages.text: Newcastle upon Tyne, UK.

passages.title: FAQ: What's your notice period?
passages.text: Three months.

passages.title: FAQ: How big a team have you led?
passages.text: Up to 12 engineers as Head of Engineering, and before that a Scrum team of junior-to-mid engineers as a Technical Lead.

passages.title: FAQ: Have you hired and grown engineers?
passages.text: Yes. I’ve hired 10+ engineers, through an interview process I designed with the CTO and Deputy Head. Many of the people I’ve led have been promoted, including one from Software Engineer to my Deputy Head of Engineering. See hiring.md and people.md.

passages.title: FAQ: Have you worked with customers and the board?
passages.text: Yes. I’ve joined sales, customer and due-diligence calls as the technical expert, been the primary escalation point for major customer issues alongside my Deputy, and reported to the CEO and CTO with board material in plain terms. See customers.md and product.md.

passages.title: FAQ: How do you use AI in engineering?
passages.text: Over the past year I’ve led an engineering department from introducing AI-assisted development to a point where the vast majority of code is AI-generated, then reviewed by AI alongside human reviewers against style and coding guidelines iterated on in the repo. See ai.md.

passages.title: FAQ: Have you owned a budget?
passages.text: Yes. I’ve owned the substantial monthly AWS budget for a SaaS platform, and managed the platform’s technical suppliers and the wider IT suppliers, negotiating renewals and contracts. See budget.md.

passages.title: FAQ: Have you led incidents and on-call?
passages.text: Yes. I set up the on-call rota and status page, led on incidents from single-client issues to full outages, and helped produce the business’s disaster recovery process. See incidents.md.

passages.title: FAQ: Do you cover internal IT too?
passages.text: Yes. I’ve been the point person for IT: the hardware estate, Google Workspace, the MDM that provisions and secures the Mac estate, and an IT service desk I set up for everyone. See it.md.

passages.title: FAQ: Have you worked with outsourced or offshore teams?
passages.text: Yes. As Head of Engineering I worked directly with an outsourcing firm in India, onboarding 5+ Software Engineers and Automation Test Engineers to bolster the in-house team. Many of them stayed for 2+ years.

passages.title: FAQ: Have you been through an acquisition?
passages.text: Yes. I’ve led engineering from startup through to acquisition, and represented engineering right through due diligence. See acquisition.md.

passages.title: FAQ: Are you still hands-on?
passages.text: Yes. Alongside setting strategy and leading the team, I’ve remained a skilled, hands-on engineer and upskilled in AI-assisted development along the way. Several of the upstream pull requests on this page are recent.

passages.title: FAQ: What industries have you worked in?
passages.text: Mostly B2B SaaS for enterprise, mid-market and SME customers, including Hive HR’s employee engagement platform and an email marketing platform sending billions of emails, plus consulting for clients worldwide.

passages.title: FAQ: Do you have compliance experience?
passages.text: Yes: GDPR and ISO 27001 accreditation, the annual audits, and arranging the yearly penetration test. See compliance.md.

passages.title: FAQ: Which clouds do you know?
passages.text: Primarily AWS, with some GCP and more limited exposure to Azure.

passages.title: FAQ: Can I get a copy of your CV?
passages.text: Yes. There’s a plain version at craigthompson.dev/cv, also as a PDF and as JSON Resume, or email me and I’ll send it.

passages.title: FAQ: Do you track visitors?
passages.text: No cookies, and nothing that identifies you. The site counts visits (the page, the country, the site you came from and which sections you saw), using its own counter and Cloudflare Web Analytics, and keeps ask.sh questions anonymously, so I can see what’s useful and fill any gaps. Both respect Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control.

passages.title: bootstrap-3-disabled-dropdown-links.md: Bootstrap 3 - Disabled dropdown links (blog post, 2014)
passages.text: A post Craig wrote on his old blog (craigsworks.com) on 2014-06-02, about JavaScript, CSS, Bootstrap, LESS. Bootstrap 3 has built-in visual support for disabled dropdown menu items as seen from their dropdowns.less file: However, these are simply visual changes and don’t actually impact the interactivity of the element itself, meaning it will still be clickable! We can get around this by utilising a combination of the [disabled] attribute (for oldIE support), and the CSS pointer-events: none rule (for evergreen browsers), a technique outlined on StackOverflow. Here’s the CSS (or LESS, SASS etc.): Once added to your styles, you can easily disable any dropdown item by applying a [disabled] attribute to the <a/> element itself, and adding the usual .disabled class to the parent <li>, as seen below. And that’s it! Your links will be truly unclickable. This will work on all evergreen browsers, as well as IE6+, though may have limited support for older versions of Opera. For more information, see the StackOverflow post.

passages.title: durandal-and-webpack-introduction.md: Durandal and Webpack: Introduction (blog post, 2015)
passages.text: A post Craig wrote on his old blog (craigsworks.com) on 2015-07-26, about Knockout.js, Durandal, jQuery, Webpack, Guide, Require.js. This series of posts will explain how to utilise the power of the Webpack module bundler with an existing (or perhaps new) Durandal application. But first… A bit of background Durandal is a mature SPA framework built atop popular existing libraries: Knockout.js, Require.js and jQuery. It allows users to use a modular, MVC-like approach to SPA development, via it’s extensive use of Require.js. This is a great starting workflow, allowing users to quickly create applications with little to no boilerplate outside Durandal itself, which lends itself well to agile development environments. Webpack is “module bundler”, which allows users to take a given set of modular JavaScript files, and compile them down into a single (or multiple) file(s). Not only that, but it also allows us to bundle in other file formats such as CSS and HTML via the use of module loaders. This effectively allows us to represent the whole application as a single, pre-built, minified file, assets and all. Perfect for production environments that need extensive caching and minimal…

Check-out the Introduction here if you haven’t already, as well as the online examples AMD Durandal’s core is written using the Asynchronous Module Definition pattern, which allows users to define their module and load their dependencies asynchronously, a must have for any web-based application. It takes the following form: For example, Durandal’s viewEngine module has a dependency on it’s own system module, as well as jQuery, and is written as: This syntax will likely comprise the large majority of your existing application code, and whilst Webpack can understand this format natively, the benefits on enclosing the whole module within a closure are lost. Since Webpack bundles the modules within the same script, we no longer require an asynchronous definition format, and can instead opt for the simpler CommonJS alternative.. It’s usage is pretty straight forward, using the same signature as the underlying gulp-watch plugin: Running gulp less will compile all .less files, and watch for changes to those watched and their @imports. passages.title: jquery-ui-draggable-exclusive-draggables.md: ui.draggable.exclusive - Exclusive draggables (blog post, 2014)
passages.text: A post Craig wrote on his old blog (craigsworks.com) on 2014-07-14, about Plugins, JavaScript, jQuery, jQuery UI. Shout out to a former colleague, who came up with the original concept behind this idea! UI.Draggable(s)… they’re not exclusive! jQuery UI’s draggable and droppable component’s are great, and are used widely throughout the web to provide consistent, well tested drag/drop functionality across multiple device types. However, one thing that is lacking, is a solid way to make draggable’s exclusive i.e. only drop on a single droppable, even if it overlaps multiple droppables! As it stands, any draggable which overlaps a droppable that is marked as active via the accept handler’s “truthyness” will have a drop event fired if the draggable is released upon it when the drag operation ends. This is problematic if you have say, four closely positioned droppables, only one of which should be dropped upon in a single drag operation. Live demonstration Drag the draggable block below over the numbered droppables. You’ll notice that it’s possible to drop onto multiple droppables in a single drag operation. passages.title: knockout-value-binding-input-number.md: Knockout value binding + HTML5 number input (blog post, 2014)
passages.text: A post Craig wrote on his old blog (craigsworks.com) on 2014-07-17, about JavaScript, Knockout.js, HTML5. Knockout’s default value binding is great in most cases, but when using the new HTML5 <input type="number" /> element, it will always return an empty string when the input is a non-number i.e. contains anything but 0-9 and a decimal! This is actually a byproduct of the number type’s WHATWG specification The value sanitization algorithm is as follows: If the value of the element is not a valid floating-point number, then set it to the empty string instead. Luckily, the specification also provides a means of retrieving the input’s value as a number, via the valueAsNumber property. When a non-numeric string is used, this will return NaN. The solution We can enhance Knockout’s selectExtensions.readValue, which is utilised by the value binding to add support for this feature where possible: Note: A byproduct of this implementation is that it will prevent people typing non-numeric characters! There’s no easy way around this unfortunately…

passages.title: qtip2-pre-release-changes-aka-what-happened-to-my-qtip-styles.md: qTip2 - Pre-release changes (AKA What happened to my qTip styles!?) (blog post, 2012)
passages.text: A post Craig wrote on his old blog (craigsworks.com) on 2012-11-20, about plugins, javascript. qTip2 is under-going to considerable changes over the next few weeks, with a new website on it’s way, a brand new build system to go along with it, and several new features and documentation updates. However, there are some breaking changes as qTip2 marches on to it’s final 2.0 release, and firmly out of nightly status! This means of course, that any of you relying on the old class structure in your code, need to update to the new classes names. passages.title: qtip2-styles-update.md: qTip2 - Styles update (blog post, 2012)
passages.text: A post Craig wrote on his old blog (craigsworks.com) on 2012-05-13, about plugins, javascript. In the recent commit today a re-factoring of the CSS stylesheets took place in order to simply the styles qTip2 uses, as well as changes to the underlying tips code to cope with these changes. The biggest change is the movement of the border and border-radius declarations from the titlebar and content elements to the main ui-tooltip element. Thanks to this, many duplicate styles could be removed from the stylesheet for a 10% size saving! This will likely effect the styling of your tooltips upon updating, and you may see black borders on your tooltip “tips” until you move the border colour declarations to the top ui-tooltip element. The ui-tooltip-shadow class now only works in IE9+ now because of this modification and removal of the IE9> filter declarations. This was done because applying a filter to any element renders the overflow property useless, as reference from this blog post comment: What I think happens in IE<9 is it “designates” a square where DirectX can render on top of a hasLayout box based on width+height properties, and if content tries to expand outside that box then…

passages.title: tether-js-transition-small-changes.md: Tether.js - Transition small movements (blog post, 2015)
passages.text: A post Craig wrote on his old blog (craigsworks.com) on 2015-09-01. I’ve been using Tether.js recently, which is a great little utility library for dynamically positioning your elements in relation to other elements on the page (similar to the jQuery UI Position plugin). I’ve recently added some additional module code, which lets you use CSS3 transitions to animate small movements of the offset nicely, leaving bigger changes to happen instantly. Note: Include this before any .tether() calls, otherwise the classes won’t be applied until the next call! passages.title: var-commas-and-equals.md: var, commas and equals (blog post, 2012)
passages.text: A post Craig wrote on his old blog (craigsworks.com) on 2012-08-12, about javascript. Working with JavaScript for a while (or any other language for that matter) you tend to pick up on a lot of nuances particular to the language, but even long time users get tripped up every now and again, as did I with a recent namespace issue involving… you guessed it: var, commas and equals! Take for example this: At first glance, it might seem as if both foo and bar variables should be declared within the local invoke methods scope, but this alas is not the case, and for good reason! Since statements are evaluated right to left, it first attempts to set the bar variable to “uhoh”, and since no bar variable is defined in our local scope (yet), it travels up the scope chain checking for a defined foo variable, until it gets to the window object, (or possibly some other scope if this is embedded within other methods&hrllip;), and sets foo as a property of that scope… we’ve just polluted the global namespace!
